extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy / history of economic thought
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and normative assessment of European colonial policy, trade monopolies, and the economic effects of slavery and capital flows in 18th-century colonies. The text articulates criteria for judging the consequences and desirability of different colonial practices and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of slaves as determinant of colony productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The profit and success of cultivation carried on by slaves depends very much upon the good management of those slaves; better-managed slaves are more faithful, more intelligent, and therefore more useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: French planters are judged superior to English in good management of slaves; protection by magistrates (more feasible under arbitrary governments) renders slaves less contemptible and induces gentler treatment, producing greater fidelity and intelligence. Example/anecdote: difference traced to legal and governmental differences between colonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governmental structure affects slave welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: An arbitrary government is more likely to provide weak but effective protection to slaves than a free government where magistrates are constrained by local electors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In arbitrary regimes magistrates can more easily intermeddle in private property management to protect slaves; in free colonies, magistrates must be cautious due to political consequences, which reduces protection for slaves and worsens their treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal protection of slaves increases their utility
rubrics_metrics.description: When magistrates give protection to slaves, the slave is treated with more regard and gentleness, approaches the condition of a free servant, and may develop virtues (integrity, attachment) that increase usefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection reduces contempt in master's eyes; humane treatment increases faithfulness and intelligence — a double-account improvement in usefulness compared with brutal treatment under fully free masters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor organization of sugar cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sugar-cane culture in colonies is at present all hand labour, though the drill plough might be introduced with advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation that European constitutionally-born persons cannot endure tropical labor; suggestion that mechanization (drill plough) could improve efficiency, but historically sugar cultivation has been organized as manual labor dependent on slave workforce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of capital (stock) matters for colonial improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The capital that improves French sugar colonies was raised almost entirely from the gradual improvement and industry of the colonies themselves; English colonies have been improved in large part by capital sent from England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: colonies that build stock locally may reflect superior conduct of colonists; English prosperity partly due to metropolitan overflow of riches rather than local management. This affects long-term sustainability and native development of the colony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motives for colonization often dishonorable
rubrics_metrics.description: First projects of establishing colonies were guided by folly (search for gold/silver) and injustice (coveting possession of lands whose natives had been hospitable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when more laudable motives (religious refugees, persecuted groups) contributed to settlement, the overall policy of Europe in establishing colonies is judged to contain little merit; colonization often resulted from disorder and injustice in Europe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many colonial enterprises were private adventurers’ projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Important establishments (e.g., conquest of Mexico, Spanish conquests) were often the projects of private governors or adventurers rather than centrally planned by European governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments frequently provided only a general permission; ventures were executed at private risk and expense. This criterion assesses the origin and responsibility for colonial expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mother-country regulations aimed at commercial monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: When colonies attracted attention, mother countries’ first regulations aimed to secure monopoly of commerce — to confine colonial markets and enlarge the mother country’s at their expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mercantilist policy tended to dampen colony prosperity; the act of navigation and enumerated-commodities restrictions are exemplars. The text treats monopoly as an essential difference among European colonial policies and criticizes it as illiberal and oppressive.

rubrics_metrics.name: General advantages to Europe from American discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Europe derives general advantages from America in two ways: (1) increase of enjoyments through new commodities, and (2) augmentation of industry via expanded markets for European produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surplus produce of America supplies commodities (convenience, pleasure, ornament) that increase European enjoyments and create new equivalents that raise demand for European goods, thereby encouraging production and industry across Europe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive trade (monopoly) diminishes enjoyments and industry
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusive trade of mother countries tends to diminish, or at least keep down, both the enjoyments and industry of other nations and of the colonies themselves by making colonial produce dearer and restricting markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monopoly confines colonial markets to the mother country and excludes other potential markets, reducing consumption and production growth. Example: enumerated commodities can be sent to the mother country only, affecting prices and consumption in other nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonies as military and fiscal assets are limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Common advantages that empires derive from provinces are military force and revenue; European American colonies have seldom furnished military force and often supplied less revenue than their maintenance costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Roman/Grecian precedents are invoked; Spanish and Portuguese colonies sometimes provided revenue, but English colonies' taxes rarely equaled peace-time expenses and never covered wartime costs. Criterion for judging colonies’ net benefit to mother country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly yields relative but not absolute advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusive trade gives the mother country a relative advantage (cheaper colonial commodities at home, improved exchange terms), but this may be at the expense of absolute gains that free trade could produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: tobacco monopoly makes tobacco cheaper in England relative to other countries but may prevent overall cheaper abundant supply that free trade would create; England may gain relative advantage while losing potential absolute benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly draws capital from other trades and reshapes industry
rubrics_metrics.description: By monopolizing colony trade, the mother country draws foreign capital out of that trade and redirects domestic capital into it, withdrawing capital from other branches and causing their decay or reorientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This revulsion raises profits in colony trade, attracts more capital, reduces competition elsewhere, and causes manufactures to be accommodated to the colonial market rather than traditional European markets. Historical examples: shift of British manufactures toward colonial markets after navigation acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly raises the ordinary rate of profit domestically
rubrics_metrics.description: The monopoly reduces competition and the total capital employed in the colony trade (by expelling foreign capital), which raises the ordinary rate of profit both in the colony trade and in other domestic trades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher domestic profits can produce absolute and relative disadvantages: selling dearer and buying dearer in non-monopoly trades, enabling foreign competitors to undersell domestically in those branches. It also forces capital reallocation effects described above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best employment of capital is that which sustains most productive labour
rubrics_metrics.description: The most advantageous employment of capital for a country is the one that maintains the greatest quantity of productive labour and increases the annual produce; frequency of returns in foreign consumption trade influences how much productive labour capital can maintain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a capital that returns twice a year supports twice the productive labour compared to annual returns. This criterion evaluates foreign trades by their turnover frequency and consequent domestic employment effects.
